concepts.title: Direct Approach for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: The direct approach learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames without architectural priors.
concepts.content: The direct approach learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames. This architecture makes no assumptions about which architectural priors are needed to compute optical flow from images. The architecture is trained end-to-end using ground truth optical flow.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach aims to minimize human bias in architecture design by allowing a neural network to learn the necessary features and transformations for optical flow estimation directly from data, rather than relying on hand-crafted geometric priors.
concepts.recap_md:
- Estimates optical flow directly from a pair of input frames. 
- Avoids explicit architectural priors or traditional computer vision steps.
- Uses end-to-end training with ground truth optical flow data.

concepts.title: Modular Architecture for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Modular architectures for optical flow follow traditional steps like feature extraction and cost volume aggregation within a trainable neural network.
concepts.content:
Another common approach is to define an architecture that follows the same steps as traditional approaches:

- Extract features from each image using a pair of networks with shared weights. This can be done by a feature pyramid.

- Form a 3D cost volume indicating the local visual evidence of a match between the two images for each possible pixel position. This 3D cost volume can be referenced to the $H$ and $V$ positions of one of the input images (generally the first frame is the reference frame).

- Train and apply a CNN to aggregate (process) the costs over the cost volume in order to estimate a single best optical flow for each pixel position.

- Use a coarse-to-fine estimation procedure where optical flow estimated at a coarse scale is used to warp the features at a finer scale to compute a refined cost volume. Then, estimate an update to the optical flow to warp the features and the next finer level of the pyramid.

(see figure: Motion estimation. (1) Extract features from each image; (2) compute a 3D cost volume; and (3) aggregate the cost volume in order to estimate the best optical flow for each pixel.)

Other variations over this architecture incorporate concepts such as coarse-to-fine refinement, matching, and smoothing. Different approaches will differ in implementation details and training. The main building blocks can be implemented with convolutional neural networks or transformers. The main difference between the matching-based and gradient-based methods described earlier is that instead of using predefined functions, the architectures are trained end-to-end to minimize the optical flow error when compared with ground truth data.
concepts.motivation_md: By mirroring traditional computer vision pipelines (like cost volumes and pyramids), these architectures leverage geometric intuition while benefiting from the power of end-to-end deep learning to optimize performance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses shared-weight networks to extract feature pyramids from image pairs.
- Constructs a 3D cost volume to represent matching evidence between pixels.
- Employs coarse-to-fine refinement and warping to iteratively improve flow estimates.

concepts.title: Endpoint Error
concepts.one_liner: The endpoint error is the average distance between the estimated optical flow vector and the ground-truth vector across all pixels.
concepts.content:
In supervised optical flow estimation, the most common loss is the **endpoint error**, which is the average, over the whole image, of the distance between the estimated optical flow vector, $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ and the ground-truth vector, $(u,v)$:
$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \right) = \sum_{n,m} (\hat{u}[n,m] - u[n,m])^2 + (\hat{v}[n,m] - v[n,m])^2$$
The sum is over all the pixels in the image. Each pixel has an estimated optical flow $(\hat{u}[n,m],\hat{v}[n,m])$.

[FIGURE:94e55f574651d9ae | A vector diagram illustrating the endpoint error in optical flow estimation. Two vectors originate from the same point: a longer vector labeled (u,v) representing the ground truth, and a shorter...]
concepts.motivation_md: To train supervised models, a metric is needed to quantify the discrepancy between predicted motion and actual motion. Endpoint error provides a direct Euclidean measure of this accuracy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Measures the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth flow vectors.
- Summed or averaged over all pixel positions $(n,m)$ in the image.
- Serves as the primary loss function for supervised optical flow training.

concepts.title: Occlusion Detection in Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Occlusion detection identifies pixels that are hidden or revealed by moving objects, which is a significant challenge in optical flow estimation.
concepts.content:
One of the challenges for estimating optical flow is that, as objects move, they will occlude some pixels from the background and reveal new ones. Therefore, together with the estimated flow it is also convenient to detect occluded pixels. If we have ground truth data, we can train a function to estimate optical flow and the occlusion map from two frames:
$$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \hat{\mathbf{o}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: Standard optical flow assumes every pixel in frame one appears in frame two. Detecting occlusions allows models to handle areas where this assumption fails, improving overall motion estimation robustness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Addresses the problem of pixels being hidden (occluded) or revealed during motion.
- Predicts an occlusion map $\hat{\mathbf{o}}$ alongside the flow vectors $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$.
- Requires ground truth occlusion data for supervised training.

slots.motivation: Standard optical flow assumes every pixel in frame one appears in frame two. Detecting occlusions allows models to handle areas where this assumption fails, improving overall motion estimation robustness.

- Requires ground truth occlusion data for supervised training.

concepts.title: Synthetic Data for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Synthetic datasets provide perfect ground truth data for training optical flow models by rendering 3D scenes with known motion.
concepts.content: The largest existing datasets are synthetic 3D scenes with moving objects that can be rendered, which will give us perfect ground truth data to train the regression function. There are several examples of existing datasets such as this, like the Middelbury dataset, which contains six real and synthetic sequences with ground truth optical flow. The optical flow for the real sequences was obtained by tracking hidden fluorescent texture. The KITTI dataset contains real motion recorded from a moving car. The MPI Sintel contains synthetic sequences made with great effort to make the scenes look realistic. Finally, the Flying Chairs dataset is an interesting synthetic dataset that consists of pasting the image of a random number of chairs over a background image. Motion is created by applying different affine transformations to the background and the chairs. These sequences are easy to generate and pay little attention to their realism. This makes it possible to generate a very large number of sequences for training, allowing for competitive performance when used to train a neural network.
concepts.motivation_md: Obtaining ground truth optical flow for real-world video is extremely difficult and often requires specialized hardware. Synthetic data provides an infinite supply of perfectly labeled training examples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses rendered 3D scenes to provide perfect ground truth for flow regression.
- Ranges from highly realistic (MPI Sintel) to abstract and easy to generate (Flying Chairs).
- Enables the training of deep neural networks that generalize well to real motion.

concepts.title: Photometric Loss for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Photometric loss measures the reconstruction error between two frames by warping the first frame using predicted displacement to match the second.
concepts.content:
One typical formulation consists in learning to predict the displacement from frame 1 to frame 2, so that if we warp frame 1 we minimize the reconstruction error of frame 2. This is achieved by using the photometric loss:

$$L_{photo}(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= 
\sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_2 (x+\hat{u},y+\hat{v}) - \ell_1 (x,y)) \right| ^2$$
where now
$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] =  h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$.
concepts.motivation_md: In unsupervised or self-supervised motion estimation, we lack ground-truth flow. Photometric loss uses the brightness constancy assumption to provide a training signal based on how well the predicted flow aligns the images.
concepts.recap_md: - It calculates the squared difference between a warped first frame and the actual second frame.

slots.motivation: In unsupervised or self-supervised motion estimation, we lack ground-truth flow. Photometric loss uses the brightness constancy assumption to provide a training signal based on how well the predicted flow aligns the images.
slots.key_passage: - It calculates the squared difference between a warped first frame and the actual second frame.

concepts.title: Learning Photometric Loss for Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Motion estimation networks are trained by minimizing photometric loss over large video collections, potentially incorporating robust norms or occlusion weights.
concepts.content: The learning is done by searching over the parameter space for the parameters $\theta$ that minimize the photometric loss over a large collection of videos. The photometric loss can also be replaced by the L1 or other robust norms. If the network also predicts occlusions, the photometric loss can include a weight that cancels the contribution of occluded pixels to the loss. The network can also take as input multiple frames and not just two.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard photometric loss can be sensitive to outliers and occlusions. Using robust norms or occlusion masks helps the model focus on valid pixel correspondences during training.
concepts.recap_md: - Training involves minimizing the loss across large video datasets to optimize network parameters.

slots.motivation: Standard photometric loss can be sensitive to outliers and occlusions. Using robust norms or occlusion masks helps the model focus on valid pixel correspondences during training.
slots.key_passage: - Training involves minimizing the loss across large video datasets to optimize network parameters.

concepts.title: Learning-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: An approach to motion estimation that uses data to learn properties and semantic cues that models cannot easily capture.
concepts.content: Learning-based methods for motion estimation address the limitations of model-based methods, which often rely on assumptions like brightness constancy that do not always hold. Modeling errors can occur due to occlusions, shadows, illumination changes, or deformable surfaces. Learning-based models can implicitly exploit semantic properties and motion-relevant cues, such as monocular depth or priors about familiar objects (e.g., buildings do not move, people are deformable). These methods can also account for approximations made in traditional computations, such as those used in calculating derivatives.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional models often fail in complex real-world scenarios due to rigid assumptions; learning-based methods can adapt to these complexities and utilize semantic context.
concepts.recap_md: - Addresses modeling errors caused by failures in assumptions like brightness constancy or rigid motion. - Exploits semantic cues and priors about object motion that are difficult to model from first principles.

concepts.title: FlowNet
concepts.one_liner: A neural network architecture that estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames using end-to-end supervised training.
concepts.content: FlowNet was one of the first approaches to use the formulation $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$ with neural networks. The architecture is simple and estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames. (see figure: In FlowNet the direct approach estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames.) This direct approach, depicted in @fig-supervised_estimation, learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames without making assumptions about architectural priors. The architecture is trained end-to-end using ground truth optical flow.
concepts.motivation_md: FlowNet demonstrated that deep convolutional networks could learn the complex task of optical flow estimation directly from raw pixels, bypassing traditional hand-crafted algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - Estimates optical flow $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right]$$ directly from two input frames. - Uses an end-to-end supervised training regime with ground truth data.
